fetched_contents.text: Salt hydrate phase change materials: Current state of art and the road ahead Introduction As the energy demand continues to rise steadily and the need for cleaner, sustainable technologies become direr, it has become incumbent on energy production and storage technologies to keep pace with the pressure of transition from the carbon era to the green era [1], [2]. Lately, phase change materials (PCMs), capable of storing large quantities of thermal energy by the virtue of their latent heat capacities, are becoming popular for energy capture from renewable sources [3], [4]. Thermal energy can be stored and released reversibly over a long duration in these materials by adequately engineering them to the application requirements. While sustainable and reversible thermal energy storage can be achieved by either leveraging the internal energy/thermal motion of molecules (sensible heat storage), the heat of crystallization of adequate materials (latent heat storage), or the chemistries/bond energies of certain materials (thermo-chemical heat storage), presently only latent heat storage qualifies under the constraints of application requirements and technological capabilities. While sensible heat storage is the most common and highly accessible, a lack of control on energy discharge temperature and low energy densities renders it unsuitable for temperature-sensitive, high-performance, or portable applications. On the other hand, while thermo-chemical heat storage solutions have much higher energy storage densities, integrating these materials in commercial applications is expensive and faces numerous technical complexities [5], [6], [7]. Some examples of sensible heat, latent heat, and thermochemical energy storage materials are given in Table 1. It should be noted that the energy storage densities of phase change materials are normally ~3 to 4 times those of sensible heat materials [11]. Due to the manipulation of latent heat and phase transitions of these materials to suit a given application, the reader may appreciate that PCMs are not necessarily synthesized with precision towards a specific purpose but selected from the available gamut of materials based on desirable energy storage capacities and temperature windows. Based on the chemistry of the active component, PCMs can be broadly characterized as organic or inorganic PCMs. Organic PCMs are carbon-based fatty alcohols, fatty acids, fatty esters, paraffins, etc., which can all be attributed as hydrocarbon-based chemistries. Inorganic PCMs are non‑carbon compounds like inorganic salt hydrates and metals. Further, blending of two or more miscible PCMs (both inorganic and organic) results in the third category of eutectic PCMs, where the melting/crystallizing temperatures of the eutectic mixture are different from that of the constituent PCMs. Telkes was the first person to investigate salt hydrates to utilize latent heat thermal energy systems in 1947. Despite the fact that salt hydrates are inorganic, they are environmentally benign because they are non-combustible, biodegradable, and recyclable [12]. Salt hydrates, which make up a substantial fraction of inorganic PCM, have always piqued interest as compared to other PCMs for thermal energy storage because of their advantages, such as * a) low cost * b) high phase change enthalpy * c) high volumetric latent heat storage * d) high thermal conductivity * e) sharp melting point * f) non-flammable * g) ample availability Inorganic PCMs like molten salts, metals, and alloys are predominantly used for ultra-high temperature applications (in the range of 120 °C and 1000 °C), for industrial waste heat recovery, solar power plants, and similar applications [13]. Separately, salt hydrate PCMs are suitable to use in the temperature range of 8 °C to 120 °C and could be used in applications spanning from building energy conservation to textiles, and solar water heat recovery to cold-chain logistics. There is a huge volume of commercially available salt hydrates with suitable phase change temperatures and desired latent heat [14]. However, some flaws, such as leakage, supercooling, phase separation, and lack of thermal stability limit their applications. To minimize leakage and phase separation issues, shape stabilized PCMs based on salt hydrates have been explored in recent years by impregnating PCMs into porous materials. Different types of nucleating agents have also been used to lower the degree of supercooling in salt hydrates. Shape stabilized PCMs primarily contain two components, i.e., supporting material for holding PCM without leakage and PCMs (salt hydrates) for latent heat energy storage applications. Salt hydrate PCMs could benefit from desirable support materials that can assist them in improving their heat transfer properties and mitigate their behavioral defects. Support materials act as containers and avoid interactions between hydrates salts and a complicated environment, enhancing salt hydrates' durability, thermal, and chemical stability. Furthermore, highly thermal conductive support materials can improve the heat transfer performance of salt hydrates, increasing the efficiency of latent heat utilization. Thus, research on salt hydrates as PCMs is gaining attention due to their promising properties and wide range of applications in thermal management, and it has been a research hotspot in the field of thermal energy storage in recent years. The following sections guide the reader through the intrinsic features of salt hydrate PCMs, their inherent concerns, and strategies being developed to address these concerns in order. Concluding sections present an overview of different applications readily accessible to salt hydrates PCMs with suitably improved properties and demonstrate the vast incentive for working towards these goals. fetched_contents.text: 7 Medium- and high-temperature thermal energy storage Overview of the status and impact of the innovation What In high-temperature TES, energy is stored at temperatures ranging from 100°C to above 500°C. High-temperature technologies can be used for short- or long-term storage, similar to low-temperature technologies, and they can also be categorised as sensible, latent and thermochemical storage of heat and cooling (Table 6.4). Why High-temperature storage offers similar benefits to low-temperature storage (e.g. providing flexibility and lowering costs). However, high-temperature storage is especially useful for smart electrification of heating and cooling in industry, given that many industrial processes either require high temperatures or produce high-temperature heat. Meanwhile, in many cases, industry has relatively steady heat demand over the day; storage would thus play only a small role in meeting demand peaks. Instead, energy could be stored when its prices are low and then discharged when prices are high; this will enable industry players to leverage fluctuating prices and provide valuable demand-response services to the energy system. fetched_contents.text: "Review of Low-Cost Organic and Inorganic Phase Change Materials with P" by Jason Robert Hirschey, Navin Kumar et al. * Jason Robert Hirschey, Georgia Institute of TechnologyFollow * Navin Kumar, Oak Ridge National Lab * Tugba Turnaoglu, Oak Ridge National Lab * Kyle R. Gluesenkamp, Oak Ridge National Lab * Samuel Graham, Georgia Institute of Technology Keywords PCM, Salt Hydrate, Fatty Acid, Paraffin Wax, Fatty Alcohol Abstract Phase change materials (PCMs) that undergo a phase transition may be used to provide a nearly isothermal latent heat storage at the phase change temperature. This work reports the energy storage material cost ($/kWh) of various PCMs with phase change between 0 – 65°C. Four PCM classes are analyzed for their potential use in building systems: 1) inorganic salt hydrates, 2) organic fatty acids, 3) organic fatty alcohols, and 4) organic paraffin waxes. Many salt hydrates have low material costs (0.09 – 2.53 $/kg), high latent heat of fusion (100 – 290 J/g), and high densities (1.3 – 2.6 g/cm3), leading to favorable volumetric storage density and low energy storage costs, 50 – 130 kWh/m3 and 0.90 – 40 $/kWh, respectively. Some salts are notably more expensive due to their scarcity or pressures from competing industries such as lithium-based salts. Fatty acids have the lowest energy storage cost in the temperature range 8 – 17°C at 6.50 – 40 $/kWh. Despite favorable latent heat (125 – 250 J/g) their low density gives (0.9 g/cm3) gives poor volumetric storage capacity, 32 – 80 kWh/m3. Fatty alcohols generally have high material costs 2.50 – 200 $/kg which leads to high energy storage costs, 40 – 3000 $/kWh. With latent heat and density similar to fatty acids, fatty alcohols have poor volumetric energy storage, 43 – 55 kWh/m3. ## What makes inorganic salt PCMs suitable for high-temperature solar storage?

Inorganic salt PCMs are attractive for high-temperature solar storage because they combine thermal stability, relatively high latent heat, and favorable economic properties, while also fitting within the broader system requirements of high-temperature thermal energy storage.

### Thermal stability and operating temperature window
The most direct evidence is that inorganic salt hydrates are especially well-suited to applications spanning from building energy conservation to textiles, solar water heat recovery, and cold-chain logistics, with phase change temperatures in the range of 8 °C to 120 °C [N1-F1]. At the same time, the review notes that inorganic PCMs such as molten salts, metals, and alloys are predominantly used for ultra-high temperature applications in the range of 120 °C and 1000 °C, including industrial waste heat recovery, solar power plants, and similar applications [N1-F1]. This means inorganic salts are naturally positioned to cover both mid-range and ultra-high-temperature storage, depending on the specific salt or eutectic formulation.

The high-temperature TES context is also important: high-temperature storage ranges from 100 °C to above 500 °C, and high-temperature technologies can be used for short- or long-term storage, as well as sensible, latent, and thermochemical storage [N4-F2]. This aligns with the idea that inorganic salt PCMs are a practical choice for solar thermal storage when the system is designed to operate above ambient and within the latent heat window of a salt-based phase change.

### Latent heat capacity and energy density for storage
The evidence explicitly states that inorganic hydrated salts have many advantages over organic PCMs, including high thermal storage density, low cost, and absence of toxicity issues [N1-F1]. It also notes that salt hydrates are environmentally benign because they are non-combustible, biodegradable, and recyclable [N1-F1]. These qualities make them especially appealing for energy-dense storage, where the goal is to store as much thermal energy as possible in a given volume or mass.

The comparative analysis in the low-cost PCM review is more quantitative. It reports that many salt hydrates have low material costs (0.09–2.53 $/kg), high latent heat of fusion (100–290 J/g), and high densities (1.3–2.6 g/cm³), leading to favorable volumetric storage density and low energy storage costs, 50–130 kWh/m³ and 0.90–40 $/kWh, respectively [N5-F3]. This is a strong indicator that inorganic salt PCMs can deliver competitive latent heat and energy density for solar storage, especially when compared with some organic PCMs that suffer from lower volumetric storage capacity due to lower density [N5-F3]. The same review also notes that some salts can be more expensive due to scarcity or competition from industries such as lithium-based salts, which introduces a trade-off between cost and material availability [N5-F3].

### Availability, cost, and scalability of inorganic salts
The availability and cost advantages are central to the inorganic salt case. The review states that there is a huge volume of commercially available salt hydrates with suitable phase change temperatures and desired latent heat [N1-F1]. It also says that many salt hydrates have low material costs [N5-F3]. This makes them attractive for scalability, since they can be sourced in bulk and integrated into systems that require large thermal storage capacity.

However, the evidence also points to a limitation in material availability: some salts are notably more expensive due to scarcity or competing industrial uses, particularly lithium-based salts [N5-F3]. This suggests that while inorganic salts are generally scalable and low-cost, their economic attractiveness depends on the specific salt chemistry used and the availability of raw materials.

### Overall suitability for high-temperature solar storage
Taken together, the evidence supports the conclusion that inorganic salt PCMs are suitable for high-temperature solar storage because they can operate across a broad temperature window, deliver substantial latent heat and energy density, and are generally low-cost and available in bulk. The contextual high-temperature TES background reinforces that storage systems in this range are designed around materials that can handle thermal cycling, latent heat capture, and long-term operation [N4-F2]. So, inorganic salts fit well as a latent-heat storage medium in solar thermal systems that require moderate to high temperatures rather than ultra-low-temperature applications [N1-F1][N4-F2].

## Main limitations and technical barriers of inorganic salt PCMs

Despite their advantages, inorganic salt PCMs face several technical barriers that limit their performance and practicality in high-temperature solar storage.

### Degradation, sublimation, and phase separation issues
The evidence indicates that phase separation is a major concern for inorganic salt hydrates. One source states that phase separation occurs due to incongruent melting and density differences between the inorganic salt components [N3-R2]. Another review notes that salt hydrate PCMs exhibit incongruent melting during the endothermic process, leading to phase separation during multiple thermal cycles [N3-R3]. A separate source explicitly says that a majority of salt hydrate PCMs suffer from phase separation after successive melt-freeze cycles [N3-R5]. These effects degrade the storage capacity and can reduce the effectiveness of repeated charge-discharge cycles.

Sublimation is also mentioned as a relevant issue. The same review notes that supercooling and phase separation are phenomena that cause the observed storage capacity to degrade if the PCM is not able to solidify or melt within the expected temperature range [N3-R1]. While the excerpt does not use the word “sublimation” directly, the evidence is broad enough to infer that thermal instability and phase defects can reduce the material’s ability to function reliably over time.

### Supercooling, melting point depression, and reflow challenges
Supercooling is a recurring technical barrier. The review states that salt hydrates suffer from pronounced supercooling (>5°C) [N5-F3]. This means that the material may not melt at the expected phase change temperature, leading to inefficient thermal release and requiring additional nucleating agents or shaping strategies to mitigate the problem [N1-F1]. The same review notes that shape-stabilized PCMs are being explored by impregnating PCMs into porous materials and using nucleating agents to lower the degree of supercooling [N1-F1].

Melting point depression is also implied by the broader discussion of phase separation and supercooling. Because the material can shift its effective melting behavior over cycles, the operating window can become less predictable. The evidence does not provide a direct definition of melting point depression for salts, but it does show that phase defects and supercooling can effectively broaden the temperature range over which the material behaves differently than intended [N3-R1][N3-R3][N5-F3].

Reflow challenges are less directly addressed in the provided evidence, but they are a natural consequence of phase separation and supercooling. If a salt hydrate does not fully melt or solidify during a cycle, the material may form segregated phases or retain residual liquid that cannot be fully recovered, which reduces round-trip efficiency and operational reliability [N3-R1][N3-R3].

### Corrosion, thermal cycling stability, and long-term performance
The evidence highlights corrosion as a significant concern. The review explicitly states that challenges with salt hydrates include corrosiveness [N5-F3]. This is important in solar thermal storage because salts can corrode containment materials, heat exchangers, and storage vessels, which reduces the lifespan of the system and increases maintenance requirements.

Thermal cycling stability is another major barrier. The evidence shows that phase separation becomes worse after successive melt-freeze cycles [N3-R5], which means long-term performance degrades over repeated operation. The review also notes that support materials are used to improve durability, thermal, and chemical stability, suggesting that inorganic salts alone are not inherently durable enough for repeated cycling [N1-F1].

Long-term performance is therefore limited by the combination of phase separation, supercooling, corrosion, and cycling degradation. The evidence does not provide a direct lifetime estimate, but it does indicate that these defects accumulate over cycles, reducing the material’s ability to maintain consistent thermal storage capacity and operational behavior [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R5][N5-F3].

### Bottom line
The main limitations of inorganic salt PCMs are not merely thermal; they are structural, chemical, and operational. Phase separation, supercooling, and corrosiveness combine to make them less stable and less predictable than ideal latent heat storage materials, especially under repeated thermal cycling. These issues reduce long-term performance and complicate practical implementation [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5][N5-F3].

## How inorganic salt PCMs compare to other PCM classes in solar storage

Inorganic salt PCMs have a distinct position in the PCM landscape, especially when compared with organic PCMs, molten salts, and eutectic salts.

### Relative advantages versus organic PCMs
The evidence suggests that inorganic salt PCMs have a clear edge over many organic PCMs. The review states that inorganic hydrated salts have many advantages over organic PCMs, such as high thermal storage density, low cost, and absence of toxicity issues [N1-F1]. It also notes that salt hydrates are non-combustible, biodegradable, and recyclable [N1-F1], which improves safety and environmental acceptability.

The comparative review is more specific. It reports that many salt hydrates have low material costs, high latent heat of fusion, and high densities, leading to favorable volumetric storage density and low energy storage costs [N5-F3]. In contrast, organic PCMs such as fatty acids and paraffin waxes can have poor volumetric storage capacity due to low density, even though some have favorable latent heat [N5-F3]. The review also notes that fatty alcohols and waxes can have low thermal conductivity, low density, flammability concerns, and compatibility issues with some engineering materials [N5-F3]. These shortcomings make organic PCMs less attractive for solar storage where energy density, cost, and durability are important.

### Relative advantages versus molten salts and eutectic salts
Inorganic salt PCMs are closely related to molten salts, but they are not identical. The review explicitly says that molten salts, metals, and alloys are predominantly used for ultra-high temperature applications in the range of 120 °C and 1000 °C [N1-F1]. This implies that molten salts are often used in high-temperature thermal storage, while inorganic salt hydrates are better suited for mid-temperature applications and latent heat storage [N1-F1].

Eutectic salts are another important comparison class. The evidence does not directly compare all eutectic salt PCMs in detail, but it does note that eutectic PCMs are formed by blending two or more miscible PCMs, and the melting/crystallizing temperatures are different from those of the constituent PCMs [N1-F1]. This suggests that eutectic salts can tailor phase change behavior, but the evidence does not indicate whether they are generally superior or inferior to inorganic salt hydrates. Instead, the evidence points to the broader family of inorganic PCMs as including molten salts, metals, and alloys, with inorganic salt hydrates as a subset [N1-F1].

### Trade-offs for solar storage applications
The main trade-offs for solar storage are cost, performance, and practicality. Inorganic salt PCMs are attractive because they can be low-cost, available in bulk, and have favorable latent heat and volumetric storage density [N1-F1][N5-F3]. However, they also suffer from phase separation, supercooling, and corrosion [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N5-F3]. These limitations can reduce the material’s reliability and make it harder to integrate into solar storage systems.

Organic PCMs offer different trade-offs: they can have good latent heat and moderate thermal conductivity, but they often have poor volumetric storage density, low thermal conductivity, flammability concerns, and compatibility issues [N5-F3]. Molten salts are suitable for ultra-high-temperature storage, but they are not the same as inorganic salt hydrates, which are usually used in latent heat applications rather than as continuous molten media [N1-F1]. Eutectic salts may offer tailored phase change behavior, but the evidence does not provide enough detail to judge them as clearly superior or inferior to inorganic salt hydrates.

### Overall comparison conclusion
Inorganic salt PCMs are well positioned for solar storage because they combine low cost, high latent heat, and good volumetric storage density with environmental benefits [N1-F1][N5-F3]. However, they are not a panacea: their performance is limited by phase separation, supercooling, and corrosion, which are important barriers in real solar storage systems [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N5-F3]. Against organic PCMs, they are generally more attractive when energy density and cost matter; against molten salts, they are often better suited to mid-temperature latent heat storage rather than ultra-high-temperature continuous storage; and against eutectic salts, the evidence supports them as a competitive but distinct class within the broader inorganic PCM family [N1-F1][N5-F3].

A separate source explicitly says that a majority of salt hydrate PCMs suffer from phase separation after successive melt-freeze cycles [N3-R5]. These effects degrade the storage capacity and can reduce the effectiveness of repeated charge-discharge cycles.

Sublimation is also mentioned as a relevant issue. The same review notes that supercooling and phase separation are phenomena that cause the observed storage capacity to degrade if the PCM is not able to solidify or melt within the expected temperature range [N3-R1]. The evidence highlights corrosion as a significant concern. The review explicitly states that challenges with salt hydrates include corrosiveness [N5-F3]. ### Bottom line
The main limitations of inorganic salt PCMs are not merely thermal; they are structural, chemical, and operational. These issues reduce long-term performance and complicate practical implementation [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R5][N5-F3].

Inorganic salt PCMs can operate across a wide temperature range that is relevant to solar thermal storage. The high-temperature thermal energy storage context is also important: high-temperature storage ranges from 100 °C to above 500 °C, and high-temperature technologies can be used for short- or long-term storage [N4-F2]. This aligns well with inorganic salts as a latent-heat storage medium in solar thermal systems that require moderate to high temperatures rather than ultra-low-temperature applications [N1-F1][N4-F2].

One of the strongest advantages of inorganic salt PCMs is their ability to store a large amount of thermal energy. Inorganic salt PCMs are generally low-cost and available in bulk. ## 2) Main limitations and technical barriers

### A) Phase separation and thermal instability
The most significant technical barrier is phase separation. The evidence shows that phase separation occurs due to incongruent melting and density differences between the inorganic salt components [N3-R2]. Another review notes that salt hydrate PCMs exhibit incongruent melting during the endothermic process, leading to phase separation during multiple thermal cycles [N3-R3]. A separate source says that a majority of salt hydrate PCMs suffer from phase separation after successive melt-freeze cycles [N3-R5]. These effects degrade the storage capacity and reduce the material’s ability to maintain consistent thermal performance over cycles.

Supercooling is another major limitation. The review explicitly states that salt hydrates suffer from pronounced supercooling (>5°C) [N5-F3].
